Thermal drone aids in rescue of injured man found at Niagara River’s edge

A man in medical distress on a bank of the lower Niagara River was rescued on Sunday morning by Niagara Falls Fire Department, Niagara Parks Police and Niagara City Cruises.

Aug. 31, 2026
Aug. 31, 2026
Updated at 2:23 p.m.
1 min read

By Ray SpiteriReporter

A man laying near the water’s edge in the lower Niagara River in Niagara Falls was rescued by emergency personnel on Sunday morning with the help of thermal drone technology.

Fire Chief Jo Zambito said at about 9:30 a.m. a Niagara City Cruises boat observed the man over the gorge wall appearing to be in medical distress and called Niagara Falls Fire Department for a rescue.

Firefighters, in co-ordination with Niagara Parks Police and Niagara City Cruises, who dispatched crew members to operate the rescue craft in high-risk waters, located the man using thermal drone technology.

Zambito said officials don’t know how the man got there, or how long he was there, but he was suffering from some physical injuries.

“He was in a lot of distress, but no one saw him go over — we were fortunate that the Niagara City Cruises boat actually saw the individual there at the water’s edge,” he said.

“When the Niagara City Cruises boat had a visual on the individual, the Niagara Parks Police have drones that actually have infrared on them, so they were able to put up a drone very quickly to confirm his location, so that we could get to him as quick as possible.”

Zambito said the technology is important in these circumstances, especially “this time of year where the trees and the bushes are very lush and it’s very hard to see individuals in the gorge.”

“The thermal imaging that’s on these drones is amazing and will actually pick up the actual heat from the body. (It’s also important) at nighttime, where it is complete darkness down there. It’s all in the interest of time, so that we can get there quicker, and hopefully the individual is fine.”

Zambito said firefighters completed the rescue and relocated the patient to a safe area so Niagara Emergency Medical Services paramedics could assess and take him to hospital for further care.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

He said firefighters are called to, on average, more than 30 river rescues per year, adding this has been a “very busy year.”

Zambito said Niagara Falls Fire Department has a “wonderful working relationship” with Niagara Parks Police, Niagara EMS and Niagara City Cruises.

“We have a great team — we work very well together,” he said. “It’s unfortunate we have to do it as often as we do, but I give credit to our staff whose training and experience is second to none — very proud of them.”

    1. Comment by Ryan.

      8 hrs ago

      Maybe it’s time Niagara asked a simple question: Would contracting policing services to the OPP be a better way to curb the culture of nepotism and “who you know” hiring?

      The Niagara Regional Police Service is publicly funded, and taxpayers should expect hiring and promotions to be based on qualifications—not family connections, relationships, or who happens to know whom.

      When cases like Edward Bednarowski’s raise questions because of his father’s connection to the service, the answer shouldn’t be “that’s just how policing works.” The answer should be transparency.

      If Niagara can get professional policing from the OPP while reducing the perception of a closed-door, family-and-friends culture, then maybe it’s time to seriously examine the alternative.

      Taxpayers shouldn’t be paying for a good-old-boys club. They should be paying for the best-qualified people to do the job
